Yes — a boom touching a shroud without damage does not count as contact

q: Starting at the committee boat end in a cross-current, your keel snags the committee boat's anchor line for a moment; you never touch the vessel itself. Have you touched a mark?
a: No — the anchor line of a committee boat is not part of the mark
o: Yes — anything attached to the committee boat is part of the mark
Yes — the anchor line marks the end of the starting line
Only if the anchor line is above the water where you touched it
why: Definition Mark: an anchor line is not part of the mark.

fig.note: Your keel snags the committee boat's anchor line

q: Finishing close to the committee boat, your topsides rub along a large fender that the race committee has hung over her quarter; your hull never touches the vessel itself. Did you touch a mark?
a: Yes — an object intentionally attached to the committee boat is part of the mark
o: No — only the hull of the committee boat is the mark
No — fenders are safety equipment and are excluded from the definition
Only if the fender was listed in the sailing instructions
why: Definition Mark: any object intentionally attached to the object or vessel is part of the mark (an anchor line is not).

fig.title: Finish at the committee boat
lines: A large fender hangs on her quarter
Your topsides rub along the fender
Your hull never touches the vessel

q: A coach RIB has drifted onto the pin-end buoy and is lying against it when you start. Your bow touches the RIB but not the buoy. Did you touch a mark?
a: No — the RIB is not intentionally attached to the buoy, so it is not part of the mark
o: Yes — anything in contact with a mark becomes part of it
Yes — the RIB is within the zone of the mark
Only if the RIB is one of the race committee's boats
why: Definition Mark: only objects INTENTIONALLY attached to a mark are part of it; a boat that drifted against it is not.

fig.title: Pin end at the start
lines: A coach RIB has drifted onto the pin buoy
Your bow touches the RIB, not the buoy

q: A safety boat has anchored about 20 m to leeward of the windward mark; the sailing instructions say nothing about her. Blue rounds the safety boat as if she were part of the mark and claims mark-room from you there. What is the safety boat?
a: Not a mark — she is not required to be left on a side by the sailing instructions; she is at most an obstruction
o: A mark — any race committee boat near a mark becomes part of that mark
A mark — the zone of the windward mark extends to cover her
A mark, but only for the boats that round her first
why: Definition Mark: an object the SI require a boat to leave on a specified side, or an RC vessel from which a line extends — not this safety boat.
ref: RRS definition Mark, RRS definition Obstruction

fig.note: The safety boat is anchored 20 m from the mark, not in the SI

q: The sailing instructions for a coastal race say: 'The yellow harbour buoy shall be left to starboard.' It is not a rounding mark of the course and lies well off the direct line. On the way out you pass it close on your port side. What is that buoy?
a: A mark — an object the sailing instructions require you to leave on a specified side; passing it on the wrong side breaks rule 28
o: Not a mark — only the rounding marks listed in the course diagram are marks
An obstruction only — a buoy becomes a mark only if you must round it
Nothing — a harbour buoy cannot be a mark in a yacht race
why: Definition Mark: an object the sailing instructions require a boat to leave on a specified side.

fig.title: Sailing instructions
lines: Yellow harbour buoy: leave to starboard
Not listed as a rounding mark
You pass it on your port side

q: Day two of a lake regatta. An orange buoy from yesterday's course is still anchored on today's first beat but does not appear in today's sailing instructions. The shortest route passes it on its 'wrong' side. May you pass it on either side?
a: Yes — it is not a mark today, because no sailing instruction requires you to leave it on a side
o: No — once a buoy has been used as a mark it stays a mark for the regatta
No — an anchored orange buoy is always a mark of the course
Only if the race committee removes it before the start
why: Definition Mark: an object is a mark only if the sailing instructions require it to be left on a specified side (or it is an RC vessel with a line).

fig.title: Lake regatta, day 2
lines: An orange buoy from yesterday's course
Not in today's sailing instructions
Shortest route passes it on the other side

q: You and Blue are overlapped on port tack, you to leeward. Grey, on starboard, will cross close ahead of both of you. Blue says a boat racing can't be an obstruction. Is Grey an obstruction to you and Blue?
a: Yes — a boat racing is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of her, and both of you must keep clear of Grey under rule 10
o: No — a boat racing is never an obstruction, only moored vessels and land are
No — Grey is an obstruction only to the boat nearer to her
Only if Grey is more than twice your hull length
why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is an obstruction to other boats only if they are required to keep clear of her (or avoid her under rule 22).

fig.note: Grey on starboard will cross close ahead of both of you

q: You are overlapped to leeward of Blue on a reach; she is converging on you. Your tactician says 'she's an obstruction, call for room'. Is Blue an obstruction for you?
a: No — a boat racing is an obstruction only to boats that must keep clear of her; you are the right-of-way boat and Blue keeps clear of you
o: Yes — any boat racing within one hull length is an obstruction
Yes — a windward boat is an obstruction to the leeward boat once they are overlapped
Only if Blue is larger than you
why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is not an obstruction to boats that are not required to keep clear of her.

fig.note: Blue, to windward, is converging on you

q: On the first beat of a Split regatta a 15 m yacht lies on a mooring directly in your path. If you were one hull length from her and heading straight at her, you could not pass without a substantial change of course. What is she?
a: An obstruction — you could not pass her without changing course substantially when one hull length from her
o: A mark — any anchored vessel on the course is a mark
Nothing in the rules — moored boats are simply to be avoided by seamanship
A continuing obstruction, because she is longer than your boat
why: Definition Obstruction: an object a boat could not pass without changing course substantially if sailing directly towards it one hull length away.

fig.note: You are heading straight at her

q: The port-tack leg of a river race runs along a stone embankment about 300 m long; you and Red, same tack, will sail several hull lengths close along it. How do the rules describe the embankment?
a: A continuing obstruction — an obstruction along which the boats concerned will pass at least three hull lengths
o: A mark — the sailing instructions require you to leave the shore on one side
An ordinary obstruction — the shore is never a continuing obstruction
Not an obstruction, because you can see it from far away
why: Definition Continuing Obstruction (2025): an obstruction is continuing when the shortest boat concerned would pass at least three hull lengths along it.

fig.note: A long stone embankment along the leg

q: You and Black are overlapped on port tack. Blue, a 60-footer on starboard, is crossing slowly just ahead, and you will pass close along her whole length — more than three of your hull lengths. Black calls Blue a 'continuing obstruction' and claims room under rule 19.2(c). Is Blue a continuing obstruction?
a: No — Blue is an obstruction to you both, but a vessel under way, including a boat racing, is never a continuing obstruction
o: Yes — any obstruction you pass along for three hull lengths or more is continuing
Yes — a right-of-way boat longer than three of your hull lengths is a continuing obstruction
No — a boat racing can never be an obstruction of any kind
why: Definitions Obstruction and Continuing Obstruction: a vessel under way, including a boat racing, is never a continuing obstruction.
ref: RRS definition Continuing Obstruction, RRS definition Obstruction

fig.note: Blue, a 60-footer on starboard, crosses slowly just ahead

q: A 29er has capsized on the run with her mast in the water, right on your line to the leeward mark. Your crew says a capsized boat is 'just another boat racing' and not an obstruction. What is she?
a: An obstruction — you must avoid her under rule 22, and a boat racing is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of or avoid her
o: Not an obstruction — a boat racing can never be an obstruction
A mark — a capsized boat on the course becomes a mark of the course
Not an obstruction until the race committee declares her one
why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is an obstruction to boats required to keep clear of her or, under rule 22, to avoid her.

fig.note: Her mast is in the water, right on your line

q: The offset mark at the top of the course is a small inflatable buoy; sailing straight at it from one hull length away, your Laser could pass it with a slight alteration. Blue, overlapped outside you, says you may not claim room to pass it as an obstruction. Is the buoy an obstruction?
a: No — a mark is not automatically an obstruction; this buoy does not need a substantial change of course to pass, so only rule 18 applies
o: Yes — every mark of the course is also an obstruction
Yes — any object you must leave on a specified side is an obstruction
No — a buoy is never an obstruction; only vessels and land are
why: Definition Obstruction: an object needing a substantial course change to pass from one hull length away; a small mark does not qualify (a committee boat would).
ref: RRS definition Obstruction, RRS definition Mark

fig.note: A small inflatable buoy, no zone shown

q: The sailing instructions prohibit entering a buoyed swimming area off the beach. On the first beat the swimming area lies across your port-tack course and you will have to tack to avoid it. What is the swimming area in the rules?
a: An obstruction — an area that a rule prohibits boats from entering is an obstruction, so rules 19 and 20 can apply there
o: A mark — the sailing instructions require you to leave it on one side
Nothing — only solid objects can be obstructions
A continuing obstruction in all cases, whatever its size
why: Definition Obstruction (c): an object, area or line so designated by a rule that boats are prohibited from entering or crossing.

fig.note: The SI prohibit entering the buoyed swimming area

q: The finishing line runs from a 25 m committee boat. You and Blue, overlapped, are finishing close to her; you will pass along her for more than three hull lengths. Blue argues rule 18 is off because the committee boat is a continuing obstruction and only rule 19 applies. Is she right?
a: No — a race committee vessel that is also a mark is not a continuing obstruction, so rule 18 applies at the committee boat at the finish
o: Yes — any obstruction you pass along for three hull lengths is continuing and rule 19 replaces rule 18
Yes — a committee boat is never a mark at the finish, only an obstruction
No — because a committee boat is never an obstruction of any kind
why: Definition Continuing Obstruction (2025): a race committee vessel that is also a mark is not a continuing obstruction; rule 18.1 keeps rule 18 on.

fig.note: Committee boat 25 m long; you finish close along her

q: You are entitled to mark-room at the leeward mark. Red, outside, leaves you a gap — but the only way to use it is to scrape the mark with your hull as you round. Has Red given you room?
a: No — room includes the space to comply with rule 31, so a gap you can use only by touching the mark is not room
o: Yes — room is any space wide enough for your hull; touching the mark is your problem
Yes — the definition of room says nothing about marks
No — because room means at least one full hull length of clear water
why: Definition Room: the space a boat needs in the existing conditions, including space to comply with her obligations under Part 2 and rule 31.

fig.note: Red leaves a gap you can use only by scraping the mark

q: 29ers at the gybe mark in 25 knots and big waves. You are inside with mark-room; the outside boat leaves you about a metre from the mark to gybe in — in 8 knots that would be plenty. Is it room in these conditions?
a: No — room is the space needed in the existing conditions, and a gybe in 25 knots and waves needs more space than one in 8 knots
o: Yes — room is a fixed amount of space, the same in any wind
Yes — a metre is always enough room for a dinghy to gybe
No — because in strong wind an inside boat is entitled to as much room as she asks for
why: Definition Room: the space a boat needs in the existing conditions while manoeuvring promptly in a seamanlike way.
ref: RRS definition Room, RRS definition Mark-Room

fig.title: 29ers, 25 knots, big waves
lines: You are inside at the gybe mark
Outside boat leaves you 1 m from the mark
In 8 knots that would be plenty

q: Passing an anchored ship, you are the inside boat and the outside boat gives you a gap of about a length and a half — enough to pass if you go at once. You hesitate, drift closer to the ship, and then need three lengths to get through. Did the outside boat fail to give you room?
a: No — room is the space needed to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; she gave you that, and the extra space you later needed was of your own making
o: Yes — the outside boat must give whatever space the inside boat eventually needs
Yes — room must always be at least three hull lengths at an obstruction
No — because an inside boat at an obstruction is never entitled to room at all
why: Definition Room: the space needed while manoeuvring PROMPTLY in a seamanlike way in the existing conditions.

fig.title: Anchored ship, inside overlap
lines: Outside boat gives you 1.5 lengths of gap
You hesitate and drift closer to the ship
Then you need 3 lengths to pass

q: Beating along a long pier, you are inside and overlapped with Blue. Blue leaves a lane between herself and the pier, but Grey, on starboard tack, is lying in that lane and you would have to sail into her to use it. Has Blue given you room to pass the pier?
a: No — room includes the space to meet your obligations under Part 2, here keeping clear of Grey; a lane you can use only by hitting Grey is not room
o: Yes — Blue is responsible only for the space between herself and the pier, not for Grey
Yes — once a lane exists, how you get through it is your problem
No — but only because Grey is herself an obstruction and must move
why: Definition Room: includes space to comply with the boat's obligations under the rules of Part 2 and rule 31.

fig.title: Pier, three boats
lines: You are inside Blue, overlapped
Blue leaves a lane by the pier
Grey, on starboard, lies in that lane

q: You are inside and overlapped at the leeward mark when Blue, outside, reaches the zone. A length before the mark Blue starts to luff you away from it, saying mark-room begins 'only at the mark itself'. Is she right?
a: No — mark-room includes room to sail to the mark when your proper course is to sail close to it, so she must let you get there
o: Yes — mark-room is only room to round the mark once you are alongside it
Yes — until you are within one hull length of the mark only rule 11 applies
No — because an inside boat has right of way over all boats inside the zone
why: Definition Mark-Room: room for a boat to sail to the mark when her proper course is to sail close to it, then to round or pass it.

fig.note: Blue luffs you away from the mark a length before it

q: You are the inside, windward boat entitled to mark-room at the leeward mark. You slow down and swing wide so that you can come out of the rounding tight and high — the tactical rounding — and Red, outside, has to sail even wider to stay clear. Does mark-room cover that?
a: No — mark-room is room to sail to the mark and to round or pass it as needed to sail the course, a seamanlike rounding, not a tactical wide-and-tight one
o: Yes — the inside boat may round the mark any way she likes
Yes — mark-room includes room to sail your proper course throughout the rounding
No — because mark-room gives room only to pass the mark, never to round it
why: Definition Mark-Room: room to sail to the mark, round or pass it on the required side and leave it astern — not room for a tactical rounding.

fig.note: You swing wide to round up tight; Red must go wider still

q: Windward mark to be left to port. You and Blue approach on port tack, overlapped, you inside and to windward of her, both in the zone. If you tack now you will fetch the mark. Does the mark-room Blue owes you include room to tack?
a: Yes — mark-room includes room to tack when the inside boat is overlapped to windward of the boat required to give it and would fetch the mark after her tack
o: No — mark-room never includes room to tack
No — room to tack can only be obtained by hailing under rule 20
Yes — mark-room always includes room to tack at a windward mark, whatever the positions
why: Definition Mark-Room: includes room to tack only if the boat is overlapped inside and to windward of the giver and would be fetching the mark after her tack.

fig.note: You would fetch the mark after tacking

q: Windward mark to be left to starboard. You and Grey are overlapped on port tack in the zone, you inside but to leeward of her, and you need to tack to round the mark. Grey is giving you mark-room. Does it include room for your tack?
a: No — room to tack is included only for an inside boat overlapped to windward of the giver; to leeward you tack at your own risk
o: Yes — mark-room at a windward mark always includes room to tack, whichever side the inside boat is on
Yes — the inside boat is entitled to whatever room she needs to round
No — because mark-room ends as soon as a boat enters the zone
why: Definition Mark-Room: room to tack is included only for an inside boat overlapped to windward of the boat giving mark-room who would fetch after tacking.

fig.note: You are inside but to leeward of Grey

q: Leeward mark, you inside with mark-room. The moment the mark is abeam of you, Black, outside, closes in hard, saying your mark-room 'ended at the mark'. Your transom is still level with the mark. Has your mark-room ended?
a: No — mark-room includes room to leave the mark astern, so it lasts until you have passed it, not just until it is abeam
o: Yes — mark-room lasts only until the mark is abeam of the inside boat
Yes — mark-room ends the moment the inside boat's bow passes the mark
No — mark-room lasts until the inside boat leaves the zone, however she sails
why: Definition Mark-Room (2025): room to sail to the mark, round or pass it on the required side, and leave it astern.

fig.note: Black closes in as soon as the mark is abeam of you

q: You are the inside boat at the leeward mark and Grey, outside, must give you mark-room. In the words of the rules, what exactly is Grey obliged to give you?
a: Room to sail to the mark when your proper course is close to it, to round or pass it on the required side, and to leave it astern
o: The right to round the mark in whatever way you choose, including a wide tactical rounding
Room to luff Grey as hard as you like after the rounding
Right of way over every boat inside the zone
why: Definition Mark-Room: room to sail to the mark, to round or pass it on the required side, and to leave it astern.

fig.note: You are inside, Grey must give mark-room

q: You are the inside, windward boat at the leeward mark and Red, outside and to leeward, is giving you mark-room. Rounding, you come down onto Red; she luffs slightly and you touch. You claim mark-room gave you right of way. Did it?
a: No — mark-room is room, not right of way; you were still the windward boat under rule 11, exonerated only if you stayed within your mark-room
o: Yes — a boat entitled to mark-room has right of way over the boat giving it until she has left the mark astern
Yes — inside the zone mark-room replaces all the rules of Section A
No — and because you touched Red you must retire
why: Mark-room is room (definition), not right of way; rule 11 still applies, and rule 43.1(b) exonerates a breach while sailing within the mark-room.

fig.note: You come down onto Red while rounding inside

q: Thirty seconds before the start you are the leeward boat, overlapped with Blue, having come up from astern. You luff slowly to well above close-hauled to make room to leeward. Blue protests that you sailed above your proper course. Does she have a case?
a: No — a boat has no proper course before her starting signal, so rule 17 cannot limit you now; only rule 16.1 governs your luff
o: Yes — a leeward boat that came from astern may never sail above close-hauled
Yes — proper course before the start is the course to the committee boat end
No — because before the start no rule limits a leeward boat at all
why: Definition Proper Course: a boat has no proper course before her starting signal; rule 17 therefore does not apply before the start.

fig.note: 30 s before the start; you luff above close-hauled

q: On the run in waves, you and Red are both on starboard gybe, two lengths apart. You sail high and fast to surf; Red sails deep and slow straight at the mark. Each of you says the other is 'not on a proper course'. Who is right?
a: Neither — each sails the course she would sail to finish soonest without the other; two boats can have different proper courses
o: Red — the proper course is always the straight line to the next mark, whatever the waves
You — the faster course is by definition the only proper course
Neither has a proper course on a run; the term applies only on a beat
why: Definition Proper Course: a course a boat could choose to sail the course and finish as soon as possible in the absence of the other boats referred to.

fig.note: Both on starboard: you sail high and fast, Red deep and slow

q: On the reach to the gybe mark you became overlapped to leeward of Blue from clear astern, within two lengths. You now steer about 10° above the direct line to the mark 'to keep clear air from Blue'. Is that your proper course?
a: No — proper course is the course you would sail in Blue's absence; a course chosen only because of Blue is not it, and rule 17 forbids sailing above it
o: Yes — any course that gets you to the mark faster than Blue is a proper course
Yes — keeping clear air is a legitimate reason, so the course is proper
No — because on a reach the proper course is always the straight line to the mark
why: Definition Proper Course: the course a boat would sail to finish asap in the absence of the other boats referred to in the rule using the term (here Blue).

fig.note: You steer 10° above the line to the mark

q: In an ILCA 7 you are alone on the run to the leeward mark in 6 knots; dead downwind is slow and gybing angles are faster. What is your proper course in the sense of the rules?
a: The course you would sail to finish as soon as possible — here the faster gybing angles, not necessarily the straight line to the mark
o: The straight line from mark to mark; anything else is above or below proper course
The course the leading boat is sailing
The compass course published in the sailing instructions
why: Definition Proper Course: a course a boat could choose to sail the course and finish as soon as possible, in the absence of the other boats referred to.

fig.note: Dead downwind is slow; gybing angles are faster

q: On the run the wind veers 20°. The rhumb line to the leeward mark is now almost dead downwind, so you sail about 15° high of it to keep speed; Grey, to leeward, says you are sailing above your proper course. Are you?
a: Not necessarily — proper course changes with the wind; if 15° high gets you to the mark soonest without Grey, it is your proper course
o: Yes — after a shift the proper course is the new rhumb line to the mark and nothing else
Yes — the proper course is fixed at the start of the leg and does not change
No — in a shift a boat may sail any course she likes for one minute
why: Definition Proper Course: judged by what the boat would sail to finish asap in the existing conditions — it changes as the wind changes.

fig.note: The wind has just veered 20°

q: You are on starboard tack approaching the windward mark, which is to be left to port. On your present course you will pass just to windward of the mark and round it without tacking. How do the rules describe your position?
a: You are fetching the mark — you can pass to windward of it and leave it on the required side without changing tack
o: You are overstanding the mark, which is not allowed inside the zone
You are laying the mark only if you are also in the zone
You are on the port lay line
why: Definition Fetching: a boat is fetching a mark when she can pass to windward of it and leave it on the required side without changing tack.

fig.note: You will pass to windward of the mark without tacking

q: Approaching the windward mark on starboard tack, you realise you will pass just to leeward of it and will need a short tack and tack back to get round. Blue, inside you on port, asks whether you are fetching the mark. Are you?
a: No — you cannot pass to windward of the mark and leave it on the required side without changing tack, so you are not fetching it
o: Yes — a starboard-tack boat approaching a mark is always fetching it
Yes — any boat that will round the mark on the current leg is fetching it
Yes — as long as you are in the zone when you make the extra tacks
why: Definition Fetching: requires that the boat can pass to windward of the mark on the required side without changing tack.

fig.note: You would pass just to leeward of the mark on this tack

q: The windward mark in this race is to be left to starboard. You approach on port tack and will pass to windward of it, leaving it to starboard, without tacking. Red says only a starboard-tack boat can be 'fetching'. Who is right?
a: You — fetching depends on passing to windward of the mark on the required side without changing tack, which you will do on port tack
o: Red — the definition of fetching applies only to boats on starboard tack
Red — a boat on port tack is never fetching because she must keep clear of starboard boats
Neither — fetching applies only at marks to be left to port
why: Definition Fetching: the tack is irrelevant; what matters is passing to windward of the mark and leaving it on the required side without changing tack.

fig.note: You will pass to windward of the mark without tacking

q: Your bow crosses the finishing line from the course side, the committee sounds a horn, and your crew asks whether you have to sail the whole hull across before you have finished. Have you finished?
a: Yes — you finished when any part of your hull crossed the line from the course side; you need not cross it completely
o: No — a boat finishes only when her whole hull has crossed the line
No — a boat finishes when her mast crosses the line
Only once the race committee records your sail number
why: Definition Finish: a boat finishes when any part of her hull crosses the finishing line from the course side; she need not cross completely.

fig.note: Your bow has just crossed the line

q: You cross the finishing line and then realise you left the last mark on the wrong side. You sail back, round it correctly and cross the line again. When did you finish?
a: On the second crossing — after the first crossing you continued to sail the course to correct an error, so you had not finished
o: On the first crossing — a boat finishes the first time her hull crosses the line
On the first crossing, but you are scored DNF for the error
You did not finish at all — a mark error cannot be corrected after crossing the line
why: Definition Finish: a boat has not finished if, after crossing the line, she corrects an error in sailing the course or continues to sail the course.

fig.note: You crossed, then realised you left the last mark on the wrong side

q: Crossing the finishing line near the committee boat, your quarter touches her hull. You carry on across the line, then do a One-Turn Penalty on the far side and sail away. Have you finished properly?
a: No — a boat that takes a rule 44.2 penalty after crossing has not finished; after the turn you had to return to the course side and cross again
o: Yes — you finished when your bow crossed, and the turn on the far side afterwards was enough to clear the touch
Yes — touching a finishing mark after your bow has crossed carries no penalty
No — and the touch means you must retire from the race
why: Definition Finish: a boat has not finished if after crossing the line she takes a penalty under rule 44.2; rule 44.2 sends her back to the course side.

fig.note: You touched the committee boat as your bow crossed

q: Photo finish between Dragons at the pin end. Your spinnaker is a metre over the line and your bow pulpit is on it, but your stem is still half a metre short; Blue's stem is just over the line. Who finished first?
a: Blue — only the hull counts for finishing, and her hull crossed first while yours had not yet reached the line
o: You — the first part of the boat to cross, here your spinnaker, counts
You — the pulpit is part of the hull and it was over the line
A dead heat — both boats had equipment over the line at the same time
why: Definition Finish: any part of her HULL crosses the finishing line; sails, poles and pulpits do not count.

fig.title: Photo finish, Dragons
lines: Your spinnaker is a metre over the line
Your stem is still half a metre short
Blue's stem is just over the line

q: P flag start. At the starting signal your bow is over the line. You bear away, sail back until your whole hull is on the pre-start side, then cross the line again. When did you start?
a: On the second crossing — you start when your hull crosses from the pre-start side after being entirely on that side at or after the signal
o: At the starting signal — your bow was already across the line, so that is when you started
You cannot start at all once you were over at the signal; you are scored OCS
On the second crossing, but only if you also rounded an end of the line
why: Definition Start: hull entirely on the pre-start side at or after the starting signal, then any part of the hull crosses to the course side.

fig.note: At the gun your bow was over; you sail back below the line

q: Downwind start in a 5.5 m sportsboat. At the starting signal your spinnaker pole is over the line but your hull is entirely behind it; the race committee shows no flag X. Did you start correctly?
a: Yes — only the hull counts; your hull was entirely on the pre-start side at the signal and started when it crossed
o: No — any part of the boat or her equipment over the line at the signal makes her OCS
No — a spinnaker pole over the line is treated as part of the hull
Yes, but only because the race committee did not display flag X
why: Definition Start: judged by the hull — the hull must be entirely on the pre-start side at or after the starting signal.

fig.title: Downwind start, 5.5 m boat
lines: Spinnaker pole is over the line at the gun
Hull entirely behind the line
RC shows no flag X

q: You hold back below the line and, three seconds after the starting signal, your bow crosses the starting line towards the first mark with the rest of your hull still behind it. At which moment did you start?
a: At that moment — a boat starts when any part of her hull first crosses the line from the pre-start side after the signal
o: Only when your whole hull has crossed the line onto the course side
At the starting signal itself, like every boat in the fleet
When your mast crosses the line
why: Definition Start: any part of the hull crosses the starting line from the pre-start side to the course side after the starting signal.

fig.note: Three seconds after the gun your bow crosses the line

q: Three minutes before the start, after the preparatory signal, you brush the pin-end buoy while running the line. Your crew says you can't be penalised because the race hasn't started. Are you racing?
a: Yes — a boat is racing from her preparatory signal, so rule 31 applies and you must take a One-Turn Penalty
o: No — a boat is racing only from her starting signal
No — a boat is racing only once she has crossed the starting line
Yes, but rule 31 applies only after the starting signal
why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing from her preparatory signal until she finishes and clears the line and marks, or retires.

fig.note: Three minutes before the start you brush the pin buoy

q: You finish in light air at the pin end, the breeze dies and the current carries you back onto the pin buoy before you can get clear of the line. Your crew says it doesn't matter — you have finished. Does it?
a: It matters — you are still racing until you have finished AND cleared the finishing line and marks, so touching the pin breaks rule 31
o: It doesn't — a boat stops racing the moment any part of her hull crosses the finishing line
It doesn't — rule 31 never applies to finishing marks
It matters only if the race committee saw the touch
why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the finishing line and marks; rule 31 applies until then.

fig.note: After crossing, you drift back onto the pin

q: Six minutes before the start — the warning signal is up, the preparatory not yet — you and Grey touch while manoeuvring behind the line. A slight scratch, no real damage. Were you racing, and can either of you be penalised?
a: Neither of you was racing yet; Part 2 still applied, but a boat not racing is penalised under it only for breaking rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1
o: Both were racing from the warning signal, so the normal Part 2 rules and penalties apply
Neither was racing, so no rule of Part 2 applied at all and nothing can be done
Both were racing because they were in the starting area
why: Definition Racing: from the preparatory signal; Part 2 preamble: a boat not racing is penalised only for rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1.
ref: RRS definition Racing, RRS Part 2 preamble

q: General recall: First Substitute goes up with two sounds. While sailing back to the start you hit the pin buoy. The new preparatory signal is made five minutes later. Do you owe a penalty for touching the pin?
a: No — when a general recall is signalled a boat is no longer racing, so rule 31 did not apply; you are racing again from the new preparatory signal
o: Yes — you remain racing until the race is abandoned or you finish
Yes — a general recall merely postpones the start; everything in between counts
No — but only if you take a One-Turn Penalty before the new start
why: Definition Racing: racing ends when the race committee signals a general recall, postponement or abandonment; it restarts at the next preparatory signal.

q: You have finished and cleared the finishing line and are heading home through the boats still finishing. Red, racing, has to bear away to avoid you. Red's helm shouts that you must keep clear because you are 'still in the race'. What is your status?
a: You are no longer racing — but a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing, so you still had to keep out of Red's way
o: You are still racing until the last boat finishes, and all Part 2 rules apply to you
You are still racing until you reach the harbour
You are not racing, so no rule of any kind applies between you and Red
why: Definition Racing: ends when the boat finishes and clears the line and marks; rule 23.1 then forbids her to interfere with boats racing.

q: Leeward gate, two marks 60 m apart, the previous mark directly upwind. You round the left-hand gate mark but pass it on its outside, away from the other mark, then head up on the beat. Have you sailed the course at the gate?
a: No — the string of your track must pass between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; go back and pass through the gate
o: Yes — a gate mark may be left on either side as long as you round it and head up to windward
Yes — passing either gate mark on any side counts as passing the gate
No — and you can no longer correct it; you are scored DNF
why: Definition Sail the Course (2025): the string of the boat's track must pass between the gate marks in the direction from the previous mark.
ref: RRS definition Sail the Course, RRS 28

q: On the second beat you pass the pin-end buoy of the starting line, still anchored, on the side you would not be allowed to on a leg it bounded. Blue hails that you have broken rule 28. Have you?
a: No — a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing has no required side, so you may pass it on either side
o: Yes — a starting mark must be left on its required side on every leg of the race
Yes — every mark of the course has a required side at all times
No — but only because the pin is a buoy and not a committee boat
why: Definition Sail the Course: a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg a boat is sailing has no required side.
ref: RRS definition Sail the Course, RRS 28

q: At 10:55, five minutes before the scheduled warning signal, the committee boat displays flag AP with two sounds. What is the status of the race?
a: Postponed — the race will not start at its scheduled time, but it may be started later or abandoned later
o: Abandoned — it is void and will be resailed another day
Cancelled — there will be no more racing today
Started — AP is the warning signal for the first class
why: Definition Postpone: a postponed race is delayed before its scheduled start but may be started or abandoned later.

q: On the second beat you are leading by 200 m when the committee boat displays flag N with three sounds. What has happened to the race, and to your lead?
a: The race is abandoned — it is void, may be resailed, and your lead counts for nothing
o: The race is postponed — it will continue from the same positions later
The race is shortened — you will finish at the next mark
The race is abandoned but the positions at the time are scored
why: Definition Abandon: a race that the race committee or protest committee abandons is void but may be resailed.

q: Blue protests you after a port–starboard incident. At the hearing the protest committee calls Grey's helmsman, who saw it, to describe what happened; three jury members hear the case. Who are the parties to this hearing?
a: Blue and you — the protestor and the protestee; Grey's helmsman is a witness, and the protest committee is never a party
o: Blue, you and Grey — everyone who gives evidence is a party
Blue, you and the protest committee, which represents the race
Only Blue — the boat that made the protest
why: Definition Party: in a protest hearing the protestor and protestee; witnesses are not parties and the protest committee never is.

q: At a club championship three things are on your mind: a club 'tradition' that nobody luffs before the start, an amendment to the sailing instructions posted on the official notice board, and a class rule limiting sail area. Which of these are rules in the sense of the RRS?
a: The SI amendment and the class rule — the sailing instructions and class rules are rules; a club tradition is not
o: All three — anything the club and the sailors generally observe is a rule
Only the class rule — sailing instructions are instructions, not rules
Only the SI amendment — class rules are a matter for the class, not the RRS
why: Definition Rule: includes the RRS, the notice of race, the sailing instructions, class rules and the national prescriptions — not customs or traditions.

lines: Tradition: nobody luffs before the start

q: After Blue clearly broke rule 10 and sailed on without taking a penalty, you protest her for breaking 'Sportsmanship and the Rules' as well as rule 10. Can the protest committee penalise her under the Basic Principle?
a: No — the Basic Principles are not rules under the definition Rule, so she is penalised under rule 10 and, if a clear breach of sportsmanship is established, under rule 2
o: Yes — the Basic Principles are the most important rules in the book
Yes — any boat that fails to take a penalty is automatically disqualified under the Basic Principle
No — because a boat can only be penalised under one rule per incident
why: Definition Rule: the rules in the book including Definitions, race signals, Introduction, preambles and appendices — but not the Basic Principles or headings.

q: On a reach your boom touches Red's shroud when she luffs slightly; you were the windward boat and know you broke rule 11. Nobody hails 'Protest' and Red sails on. What does the basic principle of sportsmanship expect of you?
a: To take the appropriate penalty promptly — here two turns — or retire, whether or not anyone protests
o: Nothing — a boat is penalised only if another boat protests
To wait and see whether Red lodges a protest ashore before deciding
To apologise to Red after the race, which settles the matter
why: Basic Principle Sportsmanship and the Rules: a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes an appropriate penalty, which may be to retire.

q: Second beat in 18 knots. A crew member of Grey has gone overboard and Grey cannot get back to him quickly. You are closest; you stop, pick him up and lose ten places. Were you required to help, and what about your result?
a: Yes — a boat shall give all possible help to any person in danger (rule 1.1), and you may request redress for the places you lost
o: No — helping is voluntary; the safety boat is responsible, and your result stands
Yes — but your result stands; helping is part of the risk of racing
No — only boats that are not racing are required to help
why: Rule 1.1: a boat shall give all possible help to any person or vessel in danger; redress is available for a score made worse by giving help under rule 1.1.

q: You have retired from the race with a broken tiller and are motoring home. You pass a windsurfer who is capsized with his rig trapped, in cold water and clearly in trouble. Since you are no longer racing, must you help?
a: Yes — rule 1.1 applies to a boat or competitor whether or not she is racing: give all possible help to a person in danger
o: No — once you have retired the racing rules no longer apply to you
No — a retired boat must not interfere with the race in any way
Only if the race committee asks you to help
why: Rule 1.1: a boat, competitor or support person shall give all possible help to any person or vessel in danger — not limited to boats racing.

q: Club race in 8 knots, flag Y not displayed and nothing about personal flotation devices in the sailing instructions. You decide to leave your lifejacket below. Who is responsible for that decision under the rules?
a: You — each competitor is individually responsible for wearing personal flotation adequate for the conditions (rule 1.2)
o: The race committee — it must order lifejackets whenever they are needed
The person in charge of the boat alone — crew have no responsibility
Nobody — lifejackets are required only when flag Y is displayed
why: Rule 1.2: each competitor is individually responsible for wearing a personal flotation device adequate for the conditions (flag Y makes it mandatory).

q: Leeward mark, Blue outside and to windward of Red, who is inside with mark-room. Blue deliberately bears away hard into Red to push her onto the mark and gain a place. What rule has Blue broken besides rule 11, and what is the penalty?
a: Rule 2, fair sailing — a deliberate breach to gain an advantage; the penalty is a disqualification that is not excludable (DNE)
o: Only rule 11 — a Two-Turns Penalty settles everything, whatever her intention
Rule 14 — contact, so Blue retires but may discard the score
Rule 69 — the only rule that deals with deliberate fouls, with a one-race DSQ
why: Rule 2: a boat competes in compliance with recognised principles of sportsmanship; a clearly established breach is penalised with a non-excludable DSQ.

q: Crowded start in 25 knots. You deliberately hit Grey, on port, to slow her down, then immediately take a Two-Turns Penalty. Grey protests under rule 2. Does your penalty settle the matter?
a: No — a deliberate breach to gain an advantage violates rule 2 regardless of the turns; the protest committee can still penalise you with a DNE
o: Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty wipes out any breach of a Part 2 rule, deliberate or not
Yes — rule 2 applies only when no penalty is taken
No — but the most the committee can do is a Two-Turns Penalty taken again ashore
why: Rule 2: deliberately breaking a rule is a breach of fair sailing in itself; the on-the-water penalty covers rule 10, not the rule 2 breach.

o: The race committee — by starting the race it takes responsibility for the boats
The organising authority — it must cancel racing above a safe wind limit
The class association — it sets the wind limits in the class rules
why: Rule 3: the responsibility for a boat's decision to participate in a race or to continue racing is hers alone.

To accept the protest committee's decision as final with no appeal of any kind
To accept the rules only while you are afloat and racing
